https://www.dw.com/en/zambia-vote-count-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IpFh Votes from Thursday's presidential, parliamentary and local elections are now being counted again Image: Moses Mwape/REUTERS Advertisement Vote counting resumed in Zambia late on Friday after it was suspended amid reports of violence against officials and the theft of ballot papers. "I am pleased to inform the nation that the security threat to the electoral process has been contained and that the necessary measures have been put in place to enable the process to continue," Electoral Commission of Zambia Chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis said. President Hakainde Hichilema is running for a second term in the southern African copper producer and is widely seen as having an advantage over opposition leader and first-time presidential candidate Brian Mundubile. Why did Zambia suspend vote counting? The Electoral Commission earlier suspended vote counting after incidents of violence targeting polling staff. It said that ballot papers had been stolen in some locations, though it did not immediately give details on where the incidents occurred or how widespread they were. After the counting resumed, the commission said the first set of results were expected late Friday night, with full results due by Monday. Can Zambia trust election referee? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video President Hichilema's main rival earlier claimed he had won, without providing evidence, and called for the results to be released immediately. Hichilema wrote on social media shortly before the suspension of vote counting was announced that he had received "encouraging results". "Let us remain peaceful, patient and patriotic as we await the official outcome from those entrusted with managing the vote," he said. Were there problems during voting? Around 8 million people were registered to vote in the southern African country of about 22 million people. Voters were also choosing members of parliament and local councillors at more than 13,500 polling stations. Local observers reported delays and frustration at some polling stations because of poor voter guidance, confusion over voter rolls and crowd-management problems. European Union observers were monitoring the election. Hichilema came to power in 2021 after defeating longtime rival Edgar Lungu , who served as president from 2015 to 2021 and died in 2025. Lungu's political legacy still looms over the election, with Hichilema's main challenger Mundubile leading an opposition alliance backed by many of the former president's supporters. http://thepeninsulaqatar.com/article/23/.text: World / Europe Germany, seven countries reject any disruption of navigation through Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb Published: 23 Sep 2026 - 08:16 am | Last Updated: 23 Sep 2026 - 08:17 am File photo of Strait of Hormuz QNA Berlin: Germany and seven other countries declared that any disruption of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait -- whether by force, threat, or the imposition of unlawful tolls or transit conditions -- is unacceptable and threatens the security and prosperity of all, particularly the world's most vulnerable. The statement was issued by the German Federal Foreign Office following the second meeting of foreign ministers and senior representatives from European and Indo-Pacific partner countries, held on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The meeting brought together Australia, France, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, Poland, the Republic of Korea and the United Kingdom. The participants reaffirmed their commitment to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), noting that the strategic environment has become increasingly volatile and fragmented since their previous meeting in September 2025. They stressed that their cooperation is grounded in democracy, the rule of law, human rights and international law, and that greater cohesion among them contributes to peace, stability, sustainability and prosperity across Europe and the Indo-Pacific. They also called on UN member states to contribute to these efforts. The participants pledged to uphold and reinforce the rules-based multilateral order anchored in international law and the UN Charter, including international judicial institutions, and to pursue UN reform aimed at enhancing the organization's effectiveness and resilience. They further underscored the close interconnection between security and prosperity in Europe and the Indo-Pacific, and pledged to enhance cooperation in addressing shared challenges, counter hybrid threats across all domains, and strengthen the resilience of their societies. Photograph: John Leicester/AP France ‘Our future is being stolen’: Greta Thunberg joins students protesting in Paris Swedish activist stands alongside French teenagers calling for investment to fix teacher shortages and crumbling schools Jon Henley in Paris Tue 13 Oct 2026 06.03 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 06.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has joined demonstrating high school students in France as the country braced for another day of nationwide protests over chronic teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling buildings . “Young people are not being included in the conversation,” Thunberg, 23, who became famous as a teenager through school strikes demanding action on the climate crisis, told reporters outside the Lycée Paul Éluard in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis. As lawyers in their robes formed a human chain to protect pupils after multiple accusations of police brutality , she added: “Our future is being stolen from us and, as we have seen here, schools are not getting the investment they need.” Now in their third week, the protests – backed by unionists, some teachers and radical leftwing opposition politicians – have shaken a government caught between calls for urgent public investment and pressure to reduce France’s ballooning deficit and debt. View image in fullscreen ‘Young people are not being included in the conversation,’ said Thunberg. Photograph: CLPRESS/ABACA/Shutterstock Marches around the country drew more than 260,000 protesters last Tuesday and a further 75,000 on Thursday , according to interior ministry figures, and are expected to be repeated on Tuesday in several major cities including the French capital. “They’re not listening to us, so we’re going to them,” the university students’ union UE – many of whose members are also demonstrating in solidarity, with an estimated 90% of France’s universities disrupted on Tuesday – posted on social media. High schools in Paris, Marseille and elsewhere were again blockaded. French authorities had been hoping that the protests, some of which have resulted in violent clashes with French riot police , would ease up and eventually fizzle out during the two-week half-term school holidays due to start this weekend. The education minister, Édouard Geffray, who has said 3,000 substitute teachers are being deployed in schools facing the most severe staff shortages, said on Tuesday he expected about 200 of the country’s 3,700 high schools to be completely closed. French media have reported, however, that at least some classes have been cancelled or disrupted in many more schools, and some lycées – for pupils mostly aged between 15 and 18 – have switched wholly or partly to online learning. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system? Read more President Emmanuel Macron on Monday called for restraint, saying the issues “deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect”, as government figures showed more than 6,800 people – mainly minors – had been detained during the protests. About 1,500 people are being prosecuted, the justice ministry has said, while 24 allegations of police brutality against demonstrators are under investigation. More than 200 teenagers, 100 school staff and 700 police officers have been injured. One young protester has lost a hand from a police stun grenade, prompting the government to ban their use during the protests, while another lost the use of an eye and a third many of his teeth from a teargas canister fired at close range. Rights groups and students have accused the police of a disproportionate use of force. Six months from a crucial presidential election to replace Macron, rival politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests. The far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, has highlighted the damage to schools and called for parents ⁠to foot repair bills, while her radical-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters ​as “incredible” and denounced police brutality. Photograph: Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images Nancy Pelosi Nancy Pelosi’s office latest recipient of letter containing white powder Former speaker is latest target of mailings sent to various Congress members in the lead-up to the midterm elections Dani Anguiano Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.47 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google California representative Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious letter” on Wednesday in what appears to be the latest incident of ill-intentioned mailings targeted at US Congress members before the midterm elections. The offices of more than three dozen members of Congress across the political spectrum have received envelopes containing white powder in recent days. One lawmaker’s office said preliminary tests indicated the powder was not hazardous. More than three dozen Congress members’ offices sent envelopes containing white powder Read more A spokesperson for Pelosi said the letter was “consistent with mailings reported by other congressional offices” and that everyone in the office was safe. “Speaker Pelosi remains focused on serving the people of San Francisco and is concerned for the members and staff whose offices have experienced similar incidents,” Nicholas Martin, a spokesperson for the speaker emerita, said in a statement. “She is grateful for the efforts of the US Capitol police, the San Francisco police department and other law enforcement agencies to thoroughly investigate this series of intimidation across America.” More than 100 letters thought to contain white powder were reportedly thought to be circulating in the US mail system. Election offices across the US have also reported receiving suspicious mail. The mailings are under investigation by the FBI, the Capitol police and the US Postal Inspection Service. The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement earlier this week: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.” Explore more on these topics Nancy Pelosi House of Representatives US Congress US crime US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
